newsitem.title: USA: Delta quarterly net edges down, ValuJet posts loss.
newsitem.headline: Delta quarterly net edges down, ValuJet posts loss.

text.p: Delta Air Lines said Thursday its profits fell 8 percent for the quarter but reached a record $886 million for the year, resulting in a $145 million profit-sharing payout to employees that was the largest in a three-year programme.
However, ValuJet, Inc. continued to struggle after a fatal air crash last year, losing $9.2 million, or 17 cents per share, for the second quarter.
The announcements follow mixed quarterly results reported by the nation's largest airlines earlier this week.

Delta, which said it carries more passengers than any other airline worldwide, said profits dropped to $301 million during the June quarter from a record $328 million in the year-ago period. Earnings per primary share fell to $3.98 from $5.77.
Operating income fell 9 percent to $519 million from $569 million.

Delta said its operating revenue rose 5 percent on 3 percent higher capacity due to robust passenger traffic levels, increased cargo traffic and the continuing success of several strategic marketing initiatives.

"Delta achieved nearly a 15 percent operating margin in a quarter with very tough economic comparisons with last year's outstanding June quarter, both on the revenue and the cost side," said Ronald Allen, chairman of the Atlanta-based airline.

"While earnings were down from our record June 1996 quarter, we are pleased that unit costs came in below our expectations and that we continue to see strong demand. We are particularly upbeat about our transatlantic performance and outlook."

For fiscal 1997, net income soared 34 percent to $886 million, or $11.72 a share, from $662 million, or $11.13 a share, in the previous year. Operating income rose 22 percent to a record $1.6 billion from $1.3 billion.

During the year, Delta took $52 million in pretax restructuring and other one-time charges for the realignment of its transatlantic and European operations announced in January. The charges were recorded in the March quarter.

Fiscal 1997 operating revenue grew 9 percent over the year to $13.6 billion, Delta said. Passenger revenue grew 8 percent to $12.5 billion on a 10 percent rise in passenger traffic, which was partially offset by a 2 percent drop in the passenger mile yield, a measure of profitability, it said.

The parent of ValuJet Airlines Inc. said it had an operating loss of $9.9 million in the second quarter, as revenues dipped to $47.8 million from $81.2 million the year-ago quarter. The airline had operating expenses of $57.6 million.
ValuJet, which agreed on July 10 to merge with AirWays Corp. in a deal that would blot out the tarnished ValuJet name, lost $9.6 million, or 18 cents per share, in the 1996 second quarter.
The merger with the Orlando, Fla.-based holding company of AirTran Airways, Inc. is subject to approval by shareholders of both companies, ValuJet bondholders and regulators.
"ValuJet continues to make fundamental progress in its plan to return the airline to consistent levels of profitability," said ValuJet President D. Joseph Corr.
During the second quarter, ValuJet resumed service to Dallas/Fort Worth and initiated the only non-stop jet service between Atlanta and Flint, Mich.

ValuJet also established a shuttle service from Atlanta to Macon and Dalton, Ga., and Chattanooga, Tenn. Also during the quarter, ValuJet Airlines joined the Sabre and Worldspan computer reservation systems with display capabilities.
On Wednesday, Trans World Airlines Inc. posted a surprisingly big loss for the second quarter, while both US Airways Group Inc. and Continental Airlines Inc. did better than Wall Street had expected.
The results lagged those of the parent companies of United Airlines, the nation's largest carrier, and No. 2 American Airlines, both of which reported better-than-expected results for the quarter.
